Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette:
Joseph had always been a man of careful analysis and steady habits. At sixty-eight, the widowed policy analyst was looking forward to a quiet retirement, a future of books and unhurried walks. That future was shattered six months ago on a Tuesday afternoon. The heart attack came without warning—a sudden, crushing weight in his chest, a pain that radiated down his arm with the terrifying finality of a closing door. He remembers the frantic call to 911, the disorienting blur of the ambulance, and the chilling sensation of his own body, a trusted vessel for nearly seven decades, turning into a hostile and unpredictable enemy. He survived, but the man who came home from the hospital was not the same one who had left.

In the weeks that followed, a new and insidious logic began to govern his life. Joseph came to believe that his body was fundamentally broken, a machine with a fatal flaw that could manifest at any second. This conviction that he could no longer trust his own body meant that safety was an illusion. His quiet, book-lined apartment, once a sanctuary, now felt like a cage where he was trapped with a potential killer. He found himself constantly on guard, his body perpetually tense, his breath held tight in his chest as he monitored every flutter, ache, and twinge for the prelude to another attack. His work, which had always been a source of pride, became a minefield; the focus required to parse dense government reports was now impossible to sustain, his concentration splintered by the relentless internal surveillance.

This pervasive sense of physical threat became a fertile ground for the memories of the attack to take root. Any sudden internal sensation—a muscle twitch, a moment of indigestion—was enough to plunge him back into the chaos of that afternoon. The memory wouldn't arrive as a simple recollection; it would detonate in the present moment. Suddenly, he wasn't in his office chair but on the gurney, the metallic taste of fear in his mouth, the crushing pressure returning to his chest, the beeping of the machines echoing in his ears. The overwhelming wave of terror that accompanied these moments was so intense that he would have to grip his desk and force himself to breathe, convinced he was dying all over again.

The constant state of hypervigilance made these intrusions more frequent and more vivid. Sitting at home, scanning his body for signs of danger, he created the very conditions for the memories to surface. The more tense and alert he felt, the more readily the images and sensations of the attack would flood his mind. This created a brutal, self-sustaining loop: the feeling of threat triggered the memory, and the memory, feeling so intensely real, amplified the sense of immediate, catastrophic threat. Each episode left him exhausted and trembling, further cementing his belief that his body was actively trying to harm him. The physical sensations of his anxiety were, in his mind, not a reaction to a memory, but proof that the original danger had never passed.

When he tried to speak about the event with his concerned daughter, the experience was jarringly different. The overwhelming emotion vanished, replaced by a hollow numbness. He could recount the facts—the time, the symptoms, the doctors' words—with a detached precision, as if describing something that had happened to a stranger in a film. This emotional void terrified him in a new way, feeding a growing fear that the trauma had burned out his capacity for normal feeling. He felt trapped between overwhelming terror and an unnerving emptiness, convinced he would never again experience simple joy or peace. It was after a particularly severe panic attack at work, where he collapsed at his desk certain his heart was exploding, that his manager insisted he take medical leave. Joseph is now seeking help, not just to manage the fear, but to reclaim a sense of safety within his own skin, terrified that he is doomed to live out his remaining years as a prisoner in his own home, forever waiting for a betrayal from within.
